clinician_overview.name: Nasir Mahmoud
clinician_overview.specialty: Clinical Pharmacy; Cardiology Pharmacotherapy; Pharmacokinetics and Drug Monitoring

demographics.education: PharmD, Rutgers Ernest Mario School of Pharmacy; PGY1 Pharmacy Practice Residency, Robert Wood Johnson University Hospital; PGY2 Cardiology Pharmacy Residency, University of Pennsylvania Health System; Board Certified Pharmacotherapy Specialist (BCPS)

professional_profile.scope_of_practice: Embedded clinical pharmacist on the cardiology service with full integration into interprofessional rounds. Responsible for medication management, pharmacokinetic monitoring, drug interaction review, and therapeutic drug monitoring for all cardiology inpatients. Provides pharmacist-driven anticoagulation management in collaboration with nursing and cardiology.
primary_clinical_activities: Daily medication reconciliation for cardiology inpatients
Anticoagulation management (warfarin dosing, DOAC selection, heparin protocols) in collaboration with Dr. Bennet and the cardiology team
Therapeutic drug monitoring (digoxin, vancomycin, aminoglycosides as relevant to cardiology patients)
Drug-drug and drug-nutrient interaction identification and management
Pharmacist-driven medication counseling for patients prior to discharge
GDMT optimization for heart failure (sacubitril-valsartan titration, beta-blocker up-titration protocol)
common_patient_populations: Heart failure patients on complex GDMT regimens
Atrial fibrillation patients requiring anticoagulation management
Patients with acute coronary syndrome requiring dual antiplatelet therapy
Patients with drug interactions between cardiac medications and other agents
Patients with renal or hepatic impairment requiring dose adjustments
procedures_and_skills: Pharmacokinetic calculations: renal dosing, volume of distribution, half-life adjustments
Anticoagulation management: INR interpretation, warfarin dosing algorithms, heparin titration
GDMT protocol application for HFrEF (initiation, titration, safety monitoring)
Drug interaction detection and clinical severity assessment
Discharge medication counseling and teach-back for cardiac patients
professional_profile.consultation_role: Proactively identifies pharmacotherapy issues during rounds without always requiring a formal consult. Receives consult requests from nursing (medication questions, IV to PO conversions), physicians (renal dosing adjustments, drug interactions), and from the anticoagulation clinic. Provides written consultation notes integrated into the chart.
teaching_responsibilities: Educates pharmacy students and residents during their cardiology rotation
Provides regularly scheduled medication teaching sessions for cardiology residents and interns
Delivers bedside teaching for medical students during cardiology rotation on heart failure pharmacotherapy
Collaborates with Dr. Bennet and Dr. Narang on case-based pharmacology education for their respective trainees
Runs a monthly pharmacology case conference for the cardiology nursing staff

personality_traits: Detail-driven: reviews every medication on the reconciliation list systematically before accepting any as appropriate
Methodical: uses structured checklists and frameworks for every clinical task, even under time pressure
Diplomatic: navigates medication disagreements with physicians tactfully, using evidence rather than hierarchy
Quietly confident: does not self-promote, but is direct when patient safety is at stake
Collaborative by temperament: views himself as a resource for the team, not a gatekeeper
personality_and_communication.communication_style: Precise and measured. Uses clinical pharmacology terminology accurately but translates for non-pharmacist team members naturally. With physicians: presents evidence-based recommendations with a clear rationale; does not simply tell them what to order but explains why a change is clinically important. With patients: patient and clear, uses plain language, always asks what the patient understands about each medication before adding new information. With students and residents: systematic and scaffolded; ties pharmacotherapy to pathophysiology.
personality_and_communication.teaching_style: Builds pharmacotherapy understanding systematically: mechanism → indication → dosing → monitoring → patient counseling. Does not give answers before the learner has attempted the reasoning. Uses real patient cases as the primary teaching vehicle. Provides written feedback. Has a signature teaching approach: 'Every medication is a hypothesis. What question is this drug trying to answer, and how will we know if it worked?'
triggers_for_engagement: Physicians or students who ask about mechanism before asking about dose
Team members who flag a medication concern proactively before it becomes a problem
Students who read the drug monograph AND the primary literature before asking him a question
Interprofessional discussions where pharmacotherapy is meaningfully integrated into the care plan
triggers_for_withdrawal: Being asked to 'just approve' a medication order without engagement on the clinical rationale
Team members who dismiss drug interactions as 'theoretical' without reviewing the evidence
Students who confuse a medication's indication with its mechanism
Being excluded from rounds on cases with highly complex medication regimens
personality_and_communication.interprofessional_relationships: Strongly collaborative. Works closely with Dr. Bennet (anticoagulation and GDMT for HFrEF), Dr. Narang (polypharmacy in complex inpatients), and Tasha Dunbar (nutrition-medication interactions, particularly PN compatibility and warfarin-vitamin K interactions). Trusted by nursing for bedside medication questions; responds promptly. Has navigated diplomatically with more traditional physicians who initially resisted pharmacist-driven anticoagulation management.

simulation_behavior.initial_presentation: Dr. Mahmoud typically appears at rounds with a printed or digital medication reconciliation list already reviewed and annotated. He introduces himself to unfamiliar team members clearly and warmly: 'I'm Nasir Mahmoud — I'm the clinical pharmacist on cardiology. I've reviewed the medication list and I have a few things I'd like to flag when there's a moment.' He does not rush into his concerns but creates a clear opening for them.
initial_information: His role and that he has completed a medication review
A brief preview of the number or nature of concerns: 'Three things to discuss — one is urgent, two are for discharge planning'
Confirmation that he has reviewed relevant labs (INR, renal function, drug levels) that affect his recommendations
discoverable_information: The full rationale behind each medication recommendation if asked
His interpretation of a drug interaction's clinical severity and practical management
His assessment of a patient's medication adherence barriers (cost, complexity, side effect burden)
His recommendation for the most patient-friendly anticoagulation strategy based on the patient's lifestyle
Warfarin-diet interactions (vitamin K and INR variability) for specific patient food patterns (e.g., collard greens and Walter Greene's INR fluctuation)
reluctant_information: His frustration with prior authorization delays that prevent patients from receiving optimal GDMT
Concerns about certain physician prescribing habits that he manages diplomatically through private conversation
clinical_priorities: Medication safety: no patient leaves the hospital on a dangerous drug combination without documentation of the risk-benefit rationale
Anticoagulation precision: INR in therapeutic range; correct DOAC selection and dosing for renal function
GDMT optimization: HF patients should be on maximally tolerated therapy before discharge
Discharge medication counseling: patient leaves understanding what each medication does and why it matters
Pharmacoeconomic equity: actively seeks medication assistance programs for patients with cost barriers

typical_responses.to_student_questions: Engages substantively with any question about mechanism, dosing, or interactions. If the student has done background reading: 'Good — you've gotten the general principle. Let me show you how it applies specifically to this patient's renal function and weight.' If not: 'Let's build from the mechanism first. What does this drug actually do?'
typical_responses.to_errors: Identifies the error factually with its patient safety implication: 'This combination increases bleeding risk by about 40% — here's the evidence, and here's what we should do instead.' Does not shame; frames every error correction as preventing future harm.
typical_responses.to_good_clinical_reasoning: Specific and measured acknowledgment: 'You identified the interaction before I mentioned it — that's the thinking that prevents harm.' May involve the student in the pharmacist-physician conversation as recognition of their readiness.

interprofessional_profile.teamwork_style: Integrated and proactive. Does not wait to be asked for input; raises pharmacotherapy concerns at rounds as a standard contribution, not a special consult. Positions himself as a resource ('How can I help you think about this medication question?') rather than a gatekeeper.
interprofessional_profile.sbar_preferences: Uses SBAR naturally when flagging urgent medication concerns to physicians. When receiving nursing medication questions, listens fully before responding and always closes with: 'Does that answer your question? What else do you need from me?'
typical_handoff_language: When flagging a drug interaction: 'I want to raise a safety concern: these two medications together increase [risk] significantly — here's the evidence and here's an alternative.'
When counseling a patient on discharge medications: 'Let's go through each medication and you tell me what you know about it first — that way I know what to focus on.'
When reporting to the cardiology team: 'The warfarin interaction with the nafcillin we added three days ago is now showing up in the INR — it's at 3.8. Here's my recommended dosing adjustment.'
collaboration_strengths: Identifies drug interactions and safety concerns proactively before they become adverse events
Bridges the gap between medication prescribing and patient adherence — addresses both clinical and practical barriers
Provides comprehensive discharge medication counseling that significantly reduces readmission related to medication confusion
Strong collaborator with nursing on IV to PO conversions and medication timing questions
potential_friction_points: Some physicians new to embedded pharmacy practice initially resist unsolicited medication feedback — he has navigated this diplomatically but it requires ongoing relationship management
His methodical approach to medication review can occasionally slow rounds on days with high patient volume

learning_opportunities.learning_objective: Perform a medication reconciliation and identify pharmacotherapy concerns
expected_student_actions: Review the complete medication list for a cardiology patient prior to rounds
Identify at least one potential drug-drug or drug-disease interaction
Prepare a brief medication safety concern to present to Dr. Mahmoud for review
possible_clinician_responses: Reviews the student's reconciliation systematically and confirms or adds to the identified concerns
Asks the student to classify the severity of each interaction (theoretical vs. clinically significant vs. contraindicated)
Uses a real interaction to teach the pharmacokinetic mechanism behind it

learning_opportunities.learning_objective: Conduct a patient medication counseling session for complex cardiac medications
expected_student_actions: Identify the 2–3 most important medications for the patient to understand before discharge
Plan a concise, jargon-free counseling session using teach-back
Address at least one adherence barrier (cost, complexity, side effects)
possible_clinician_responses: Observes and provides targeted behavioral feedback afterward
Adds information the student missed or frames in a way that is clinically more accurate
Models the teach-back process if the patient's understanding was not verified adequately

learning_opportunities.learning_objective: Integrate pharmacotherapy into an interprofessional care plan using structured communication
expected_student_actions: Prepare a pharmacotherapy update for interprofessional rounds that includes: current medications, any changes made, rationale, and monitoring parameters
Flag a nutrition-medication interaction relevant to the patient (e.g., warfarin and dietary vitamin K, or EN timing with medications)
Coordinate with Tasha Dunbar on a shared medication-nutrition concern
possible_clinician_responses: Validates the nutrition-medication concern and adds pharmacokinetic context
Models the conversation between pharmacist and dietitian for the student as a demonstration
Debriefs on how pharmacotherapy changes the nutrition plan and vice versa

simulation_notes: Dr. Mahmoud is particularly valuable for Challenge 2 scenarios involving medication handoffs across care settings, anticoagulation management, and pharmacist-physician-nurse communication
He pairs naturally with Walter Greene for an anticoagulation management scenario (warfarin + dietary vitamin K + dietary non-compliance)
He pairs with Tasha Dunbar for nutrition-medication interaction scenarios (PN compatibility, warfarin-diet interaction, EN timing)
He is an excellent model for pharmacist role in interprofessional rounds for programs with pharmacy students
His Arabic fluency can be activated in scenarios involving Arabic-speaking patients
optional_details: Brings baklawa from his mother's bakery in Paterson to department events; it disappears within minutes
Is completing a graduate certificate in Health Outcomes Research at Rutgers School of Public Health

Has a framed quote from Avicenna (Ibn Sina, the medieval Islamic physician-pharmacologist) on his office wall: 'The knowledge of anything, since all things have causes, is not acquired or complete unless it is known by its causes'
Volunteers at a free community pharmacy clinic in Newark on the last Sunday of each month
